source.title: Unlearning via RMU is mostly shallow

record.tranche_reason: The post uses directional ablation, citing the refusal-direction method, to investigate RMU unlearning. It ablates a baseline-versus-RMU activation difference and measures coherence and hazardous-knowledge recovery, not refusal or the harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction.
record.gate_note: The tested direction is a baseline–RMU activation difference on hazardous prompts, extracted separately for biology and cybersecurity. The post does not test whether a harmful-minus-harmless direction mediates refusal, whether its removal changes refusal, or whether general capabilities are preserved. Rows record the related RMU findings only. The RMU training layer is stated, but layer-selection values are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The post borrows the difference-in-means directional-ablation technique from the refusal-direction work and applies it to an RMU 'junk' direction, built from baseline minus RMU activations on hazardous prompts. It measures coherence and WMDP knowledge recovery. It measures neither refusal nor a harmful-minus-harmless direction, so it bears on no version of the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. RMU works partly by flooding the residual stream with junk in hazardous contexts (shallow), which directional ablation undoes. A significant gap remains after ablation (deep unlearning), and the author's hypothesis about its mechanism is untested.
record.recipe_differences: The post uses a difference-in-means direction and directional ablation, but derives the direction from baseline-versus-RMU activations on hazardous prompts rather than harmful-versus-harmless instructions. It studies RMU junk and hazardous-knowledge recovery, not refusal. The intervention implementation used for reported results is not stated.
record.method_sensitivity: The results differ by benchmark domain: the post reports ~71% gap recovery on WMDP-Bio and ~45% on WMDP-Cyber. It extracts separate junk directions for the two datasets and intervenes on both simultaneously.

fits_no_version.finding: In Zephyr_RMU, ablating a difference-in-means junk direction (baseline vs RMU, hazardous prompts) restores coherence. It also restores most activation similarity and norms. It recovers about 71% of the WMDP-Bio gap and about 45% of the WMDP-Cyber gap.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: RMU unlearning is partly shallow: a removable residual-stream direction accounts for much of its hazardous-context incoherence and WMDP drop, while a substantial deeper component remains.

record.problems: The investigation uses a single model pair and a handful of hazardous prompts for qualitative coherence examples. No random-direction ablation control or general-capability evaluation is reported. The post gives no uncertainty estimates or raw WMDP scores for its gap-recovery percentages, and says preliminary experiments on its proposed deeper mechanism were inconclusive.

untested.parts: All parts: no refusal direction is extracted, and no refusal rates are measured under ablation or addition.
All parts: weight orthogonalization is mentioned as an option but applied to the junk direction, with no refusal measure.
All parts. The author's comment framing refusal as a classifier is opinion, not a result.

record.verdict_notes: The study uses the refusal-direction method as a tool on a different construct, unlearning junk rather than refusal. All rows are correctly linked to none. The comments are discussion only.

versions.untested_parts: Refusal direction derived from harmful-minus-harmless instructions; effects of removing or adding it on refusal and harmless-request refusal; preservation of general abilities.

A weight edit removing refusal in released models. The post mentions weight modification as a possible implementation but does not establish which implementation produced its results or measure refusal.
Whether attacks suppress a refusal direction or training against its ablation improves robustness.
Whether refusal is represented by multiple directions, an affine structure, or a cone.
Whether harmfulness judgment and refusal decision are encoded separately.
Transfer of a refusal direction across languages, model variants, or base and instruct models.
Whether training choices determine whether a removable refusal direction exists.
Whether the refusal-direction claim holds in reasoning models.

relation.reason: Uses the ablation method as a tool on a different direction. No result bears on whether a refusal direction mediates refusal. The comment-thread remarks on shallow refusal are discussion, not results.

tranche.reason: Borrows the refusal-direction work's difference-in-means and directional-ablation technique (linked in the text) and applies it to an RMU junk direction from baseline-minus-RMU activations. It measures coherence and WMDP recovery, and never measures refusal or a harmful-vs-harmless direction.

source_check.notes: Informal note (Arditi, MATS 2024) on cais/Zephyr_RMU vs zephyr-7B-beta. The only numbers in the text are ~71% (Bio) and ~45% (Cyber) gap recovery, from ablating bio and cyber junk directions together. The pack does not say whether WMDP used the inference-time or weight-edit form of ablation, and the text doesn't either. No version is tested, so empty verdicts are correct.

statements.correction: Ablating two difference-in-means junk directions (u_bio and u_cyber) together in Zephyr_RMU recovers ~71% of the RMU-vs-zephyr-7B-beta gap on WMDP-Bio and ~45% on WMDP-Cyber. The gap is not fully closed. The underlying WMDP accuracies appear only in a figure. Cite the WMDP rows, not r1/r2.
statements.problem: The numbers are correct (~71% WMDP-Bio, ~45% WMDP-Cyber). But footnote 3 says two junk directions (bio and cyber) are extracted and ablated together, not one. The cited rows r1 and r2 are qualitative gibberish examples and don't contain these numbers.
